what_it_does: Intel's SGX and TDX are technologies that create a locked-off secure compartment (sometimes called a trusted execution environment, or TEE) inside a processor, meant to protect sensitive code and data even from a compromised operating system or cloud host. One known attack is to watch how much power the CPU draws during computation — patterns in power consumption can leak secrets like encryption keys. Intel tried to block this by filtering access to the processor's built-in power-measurement registers (special control registers called MSRs). This paper reveals that the filtering only covers 'in-band' measurements — readings made through the normal software interface — while leaving open an 'out-of-band' path used by server management firmware to read energy counters through a separate hardware channel called the Package Configuration Space. The authors reverse-engineered that management communication protocol, exploited it to read energy data outside the filter, and then used a timing trick (deliberately disabling the filtered MSRs to create a synchronization signal) to align those out-of-band readings with the secure compartment's execution, successfully extracting secret information from SGX and TDX environments.
